input: Over the course of one quarter, a defect-reduction project on a packing line successfully reduced the reject rate from 4% to 1.7%, which represents a reduction of some 2.3 percentage points. This is a meaningful improvement in the performance of the line, because the reject rate captures the proportion of packed units that fail to meet the required standard and have to be removed from the output. Based on an annual volume of 137k units per year, it is estimated that this change will avoid approximately 3151 rejected units per year, which is a substantial saving in terms of wasted product, wasted packaging and wasted effort across the operation as a whole. The avoided figure is obtained by applying the difference between the two reject rates to the annual volume, so it rests on the assumption that the improved rate achieved during the quarter can be sustained across the full year and across the full mix of products handled by the line. It should also be noted that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the reported rates have not been adjusted in any way to account for it, so the comparison should be read with that in mind. Overall, the results demonstrate a clear improvement in line performance over the period, although the figures should be understood as applying to the conditions under which they were measured, including the shutdown that formed part of the quarter. Further monitoring over subsequent quarters will show whether the improvement is maintained once the line has returned to its normal pattern of operation.
target: The packing line reject rate fell from 4% to 1.7% over one quarter, a reduction of 2.3 percentage points. At the stated volume of 137k units per year, the reduction avoids about 3151 rejected units per year. The reject rate is the count of rejected units divided by the units packed over the same period, so the two rates compare the line with itself on one counting basis. A rejected unit is a packed unit removed from the output as defective, and the avoided count is the number of such units the lower rate removes from a year of production at the stated volume. The avoided count is derived from the two rates and the annual volume: the earlier rate applied to the volume gives the rejections the year would have carried, the later rate gives the rejections it now carries, and the difference is the saving. The saving is stated per year because the volume is stated per year; the rates themselves were measured over one quarter. Carrying a quarter's rates across a full year assumes the product mix and the running pattern of the quarter stand for the year, and the figure inherits that assumption. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The comparison therefore stands as measured: no allowance has been added for the shutdown, and any reader who needs rates on a running-time basis must restate them before use. The claim is limited to the two rates, the stated volume and the period in which the rates were measured. The two rates and the volume are reported together, so that the avoided count can be recomputed from them by any reader of the case.
